title: Screens at Home and Spectacles in Theaters
summary: When television arrived, movie theaters had to fight to keep their audiences. They tried giant curved screens, 3D glasses and films so big they ran sideways through the projector. Meanwhile, tape let people record TV at home, and computers learned to create dinosaurs and talking toys.

sections.heading: The Box That Emptied the Cinemas
paragraphs: Picture an American family in 1946. On a Saturday night, going to the movies is what almost everyone does. There is a newsreel, a cartoon, maybe two feature films, all for the price of a ticket. Movies are the biggest entertainment in the country.

Now jump forward ten years. The same family is sitting at home in the living room, watching a small, flickering black-and-white screen set inside a wooden cabinet. In 1948, only about 1 in every 100 American homes had a television. By 1955, about three out of every four did. That is one of the fastest changes in daily life the world had ever seen.

For Hollywood, it felt like an earthquake. By one widely quoted count, movie attendance in the United States fell from about 90 million in 1948 to about 46 million in 1951. Why pay for a ticket, find parking and hire a babysitter, when comedy shows, sports and news came into your house for free? At the same time, a 1948 court case known as the Paramount decision forced the big studios to sell their chains of theaters, which shook up the business even more.

The studios asked themselves a simple question: what can a cinema do that a small TV screen cannot? Their answer was spectacle. Theaters would offer pictures that were bigger, wider, brighter, louder and even three-dimensional. The 1950s became a decade of wild experiments, some brilliant, some short-lived and a few just plain silly. One 1960 film, Scent of Mystery, even pumped smells into the theater in a system called Smell-O-Vision. It did not catch on.

sections.heading: Wider, Wider, Widest
paragraphs: On 30 September 1952, an audience at the Broadway Theatre in New York sat down in front of a deeply curved screen. The film, This Is Cinerama, began with an ordinary-sized black-and-white picture. Then the curtains swept open, the screen grew enormous, and the audience found themselves riding at the front of a roller coaster. People gripped their seats as if they were really falling down the drops.

Cinerama was invented by Fred Waller, who had earlier worked on special effects and on a multi-projector system to train aircraft gunners. Cinerama used three cameras filming side by side. In the theater, three projectors, each in its own booth, threw three pictures onto a giant screen curved around the audience so that it filled about 146 degrees of their view, close to the edge of what your eyes can see without turning your head. A seven-track sound system with speakers behind the screen and around the hall, developed by Hazard E. Reeves, made sounds move from one side to the other.

Cinerama was thrilling, but it was difficult. The joins between the three pictures could be seen as faint lines, and things close to the camera could look bent where the pictures met. Only special theaters could afford the equipment. Most Cinerama films were travel adventures that flew over oceans and mountains. Only two told regular stories with actors, including How the West Was Won (1962), after which the three-camera system was dropped.

The 20th Century Fox studio wanted something cheaper that ordinary theaters could install. They found it in an invention from the 1920s by a French scientist, Henri Chrétien, who had designed a special lens called the Hypergonar. Fox named the system CinemaScope. The trick is called anamorphic, from Greek words meaning 'formed again'. When filming, a special lens squeezes a wide scene sideways so it fits onto a normal 35mm frame. On the film itself, everything looks tall and skinny, like a reflection in a funhouse mirror. In the theater, a matching lens on the projector stretches the picture back out to its proper width.

The first CinemaScope film, The Robe, a story set in ancient Rome starring Richard Burton, premiered at the Roxy Theatre in New York on 16 September 1953. Its picture was about two and a half times as wide as it was tall, compared with the nearly square shape of older films and TV screens. The Robe was a huge hit, and soon many studios were making 'Scope' films. Early CinemaScope lenses had a funny flaw: in close-ups, faces could look puffed out sideways, a problem nicknamed 'the mumps'. Later lenses from a company called Panavision fixed this, and Panavision lenses became the standard.

Another widescreen method simply used wider film. Todd-AO, first used for the musical Oklahoma! (1955), ran film 70mm wide, giving a sharper and brighter picture. The shape of today's movie screens, and even of the TV in your living room, comes from this 1950s battle to look wider than television.

sections.heading: Glasses On: The First 3D Craze
paragraphs: If wider was good, what about deeper? On 26 November 1952, a film called Bwana Devil opened in Los Angeles. Its makers promised that lions would seem to leap right off the screen. Audiences put on gray cardboard glasses and gasped. The film was not considered very good, but it made a lot of money and started the first big 3D craze in American movies.

How does 3D work? Your two eyes are a few centimeters apart, so each sees the world from a slightly different angle. Your brain combines the two views and works out how far away things are. A 3D film is shot with two cameras placed side by side, like two eyes. In the theater, the two films are projected together through filters that send the light waves vibrating in different directions. This is called polarization. The lenses of your glasses are polarizing filters too, each letting through only one of the pictures, so your left eye sees the left camera's view and your right eye sees the right camera's view. Your brain does the rest.

For a few years, 3D was everywhere. Warner Bros.' horror film House of Wax (1953), starring Vincent Price, was a big success, and many westerns, monster movies and even musicals were made in 3D. But the craze faded quickly. The two projectors had to stay perfectly in step, or the picture became blurry and gave people headaches. The glasses made the picture dimmer. And CinemaScope offered a sense of size without any glasses at all. By the mid-1950s, most 3D films were being shown flat. 3D would return in waves over the following decades, with its biggest comeback arriving in the digital age.

sections.heading: Pictures on a Ribbon of Magnetic Tape
paragraphs: Early television had a big problem. Most shows were broadcast live, as they happened. That was fine in New York, but the United States stretches across several time zones. A news program shown at 6:30 in the evening on the East Coast would reach California in the middle of the afternoon. To replay shows later, networks filmed a TV screen with a movie camera, rushed the film through developing, and broadcast it a few hours later. These blurry copies were called kinescopes.

Engineers knew that sound could already be recorded on magnetic tape, a plastic ribbon coated with tiny magnetic particles. Video was much harder, because a TV picture contains vastly more information each second than sound. Pulling tape past a recording head fast enough would need miles of tape. At the Ampex company in California, a small team including Charles Ginsburg and a young engineer named Ray Dolby, who later became famous for Dolby sound, found a clever solution. Instead of moving the tape incredibly fast, they spun the recording heads. Four heads sat on a wheel spinning more than 14,000 times a minute, sweeping across tape 2 inches wide. Each sweep wrote a thin stripe of picture information.

Ampex showed its machine at a broadcasters' convention in Chicago on 14 April 1956. The audience saw a recording played back moments after it was made, and it looked almost as good as live TV. They burst into applause. The machine was huge and cost about $45,000 at the time, yet TV networks lined up to buy it. On 30 November 1956, CBS used videotape to delay its evening news program, Douglas Edwards and the News, for viewers in the West. Within a few years, videotape had changed television, allowing shows to be recorded, edited and repeated.

Home video came next. In 1975, Sony launched Betamax, a video cassette recorder (VCR) for the home. In 1976, the Japanese company JVC launched a rival called VHS. The two kinds of tape did not fit in each other's machines, so shoppers had to pick one. This contest became known as the videotape format war. Betamax often had a slightly sharper picture, but early VHS tapes could record for two hours instead of one, long enough for a whole movie or a football game. Many companies made VHS machines, which helped bring prices down. By 1987, VHS held about 90 percent of the American VCR market, and in 1988 Sony itself started selling VHS machines.

Hollywood studios were at first alarmed that people could copy TV shows and films at home. Universal Studios and Disney sued Sony. In 1984, in a case often called the Betamax case, the US Supreme Court ruled that recording a program at home to watch later was allowed. Soon studios discovered they could make huge sums by selling and renting tapes. Video rental shops appeared in towns everywhere, and a Friday night trip to pick a movie became a family ritual.

Then came the camcorder, a camera and video recorder combined into one machine you could hold. Sony's Betamovie, released in 1983, was one of the first for consumers; it could record but not play back. JVC released smaller VHS-C cameras the same year, and in 1985 Sony introduced the compact Video8 format. For the first time, ordinary families could record long stretches of moving pictures with sound and play them instantly on the TV, with no film to develop. Birthday parties, school plays and baby's first steps were suddenly captured on tape.

sections.heading: IMAX: A Frame Ten Times Bigger
paragraphs: While some inventors made screens smaller and more personal, a group of Canadians went in the opposite direction. In 1967, filmmakers Graeme Ferguson, Roman Kroitor and Robert Kerr, together with engineer William C. Shaw, founded a company to build the biggest, sharpest movie system in the world. At first it was called Multiscreen Corporation. They later chose a catchier name: IMAX, short for 'Image Maximum'.

Their first film, Tiger Child, was shown at Expo '70, the world's fair in Osaka, Japan, in 1970. The first permanent IMAX theater opened in May 1971 at the Cinesphere, a dome-shaped building at Ontario Place in Toronto.

The secret of IMAX is the size of each frame. Normal 35mm film runs vertically through the projector, and each frame is a little larger than a postage stamp. IMAX uses film 70mm wide, but turns it sideways. The film runs horizontally, and each frame stretches across 15 of the little sprocket holes along the edge, rather than 4 or 5. The result is a frame about ten times the area of a standard 35mm movie frame. More area means more detail, so the picture stays sharp even on a screen several stories tall.

Moving such big frames smoothly was a serious engineering challenge. Normal projectors yank the film forward with a claw, as you read in Part 11, but that would tear heavy IMAX film. William Shaw adapted an idea from an Australian inventor called the rolling loop, in which the film moves in a gentle wave, and added puffs of compressed air to help each frame settle into place. Each frame is held perfectly flat against the lens by suction for its moment on the screen.

In 1973, a version for dome-shaped theaters, first called OMNIMAX, opened in San Diego, wrapping the picture overhead like a planetarium sky. IMAX became famous for nature and science films: flights through the Grand Canyon, journeys under the sea and even footage filmed by astronauts aboard the Space Shuttle, using IMAX cameras carried into orbit.

sections.heading: Spaceships on a Robot Arm
paragraphs: In 1975, a young director named George Lucas had a problem. He was planning a space adventure called Star Wars, full of space battles, and no special effects company could make the shots he imagined. So, on 26 May 1975, he started his own. A team led by John Dykstra set up in a warehouse in Van Nuys, California. They named themselves Industrial Light & Magic, or ILM.

Their most important tool was a camera rig nicknamed the Dykstraflex, built in 1976. It is often called the first digital motion-control camera system. A camera was mounted on a long, motorized arm and track, controlled by a computer. It could move in seven different ways, sliding along, rising, tilting, turning and rolling, while the computer also controlled the focus and the shutter.

Why did that matter? A space battle shot is made by filming many separate things: an X-wing model, a TIE fighter model, glowing engines, a background of stars. Each piece is filmed separately, usually in front of a blue screen so it can be cut out later, and then all the pieces are combined into one picture, a process called compositing. For the pieces to fit together, the camera has to make exactly the same movement every time. A human operator can never repeat a move perfectly. The Dykstraflex could, again and again, as many times as needed. The models themselves barely moved; it was the camera that swooped past them, creating the feeling of high-speed flight.

Star Wars opened on 25 May 1977 and became one of the most successful films ever made. Audiences had never seen spaceships fly like that. Dykstra and two colleagues, Alvah Miller and Jerry Jeffress, who built the electronics, received Academy Awards for the system. ILM went on to create effects for hundreds of films and became one of the most important effects companies in the world.
Notice something about this story: Star Wars mostly still used real models, real cameras and real film. The computer was the camera's brain, not the artist. That was about to change.

sections.heading: Computers Learn to Draw
paragraphs: Computer graphics, often called CGI (computer-generated imagery), means pictures created by a computer from mathematical descriptions of shapes, colors and light, rather than photographed from real objects. In the 1970s, computers were slow and huge, and making even a simple image took enormous effort. Early movies used CGI for small things, like screens in the background.

Then, on 9 July 1982, Disney released Tron, directed by Steven Lisberger, about a programmer who is pulled inside a computer world. Four computer graphics companies made about 15 to 20 minutes of computer animation for it, including racing light cycles that zoomed at sharp right angles. Much of the glowing look, however, was made by hand, by filming actors in black-and-white and then coloring the light through the film frame by frame in a technique called backlit animation. Tron was not nominated for a visual effects Oscar. Later, the scientist Ken Perlin, who had worked on it, won a technical Academy Award in 1997 for 'Perlin noise', a method for making computer surfaces look naturally rough, like clouds, marble or wood, which became used all over the film industry.

The same summer, Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan (1982) included a sequence of about a minute showing a dead, rocky planet bursting into life, with fire sweeping across its surface and oceans and forests spreading behind it. It was made by the young computer graphics team at Lucasfilm, the company George Lucas had set up alongside ILM. To make the flames, the team invented a way of drawing thousands of tiny moving points, called a particle system, an idea still used today for fire, smoke, rain, sparks and magic spells in films and video games. Each new trick added a tool to the computer artist's toolbox, and the people who invented those tools would soon become famous in their own right.

In 1985, the film Young Sherlock Holmes included a scene in which a knight made of pieces of a stained-glass window steps out of the window and walks toward a priest. It is often called the first fully computer-generated, realistic character in a feature film. It was created by the computer graphics group at Lucasfilm, George Lucas's company, with animator John Lasseter. The shot lasts only a few seconds, but it showed that a computer could make a believable character move. In 1989, ILM created a watery tentacle that imitated people's faces in The Abyss, and in 1991 a liquid-metal villain called the T-1000 in Terminator 2: Judgment Day.

The biggest leap came with dinosaurs. Steven Spielberg planned Jurassic Park using giant robot dinosaurs made by Stan Winston's team, plus stop-motion style puppets by the animator Phil Tippett for full-body shots. Winston's life-size Tyrannosaurus rex was about 20 feet (6 meters) tall and weighed about 9,000 pounds (4 tonnes). But at ILM, animators Steve Williams and Mark Dippé secretly experimented with computer dinosaurs. When Spielberg saw a test of a computer T. rex walking in daylight, he was so impressed that he switched the full-body shots to CGI.

Tippett, a stop-motion master, reportedly joked, 'I think I'm extinct.' Spielberg liked the line so much he put it into the film's script. Tippett did not lose his job, though. His team helped build the Dinosaur Input Device, a dinosaur-shaped puppet skeleton covered in sensors. When animators posed the puppet, the computer copied the pose into the digital dinosaur, combining old-fashioned animation skill with new technology.

Jurassic Park was released on 11 June 1993. Of its about 15 minutes of dinosaur screen time, roughly 9 minutes were Stan Winston's animatronics and only about 6 minutes were CGI. Yet those 6 minutes changed filmmaking. The film earned well over $900 million in its first run and won three Academy Awards, including for visual effects. After Jurassic Park, filmmakers knew they could put almost anything they could imagine on the screen.

sections.heading: To Infinity and Beyond: Toy Story
paragraphs: Remember the Lucasfilm computer group that made the stained-glass knight? In 1986, it was sold to Steve Jobs, the co-founder of Apple, and became an independent company called Pixar. At first Pixar mainly sold an expensive image computer and made TV commercials. But John Lasseter kept making short films to show what computer animation could do. His 1988 short Tin Toy, about a wind-up toy band fleeing a drooling baby, won the 1989 Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film, the first computer-animated film to do so. That success convinced Disney to make a deal with Pixar for a full-length film.

The result was Toy Story, directed by Lasseter, about a cowboy doll named Woody and a space-ranger toy named Buzz Lightyear, voiced by Tom Hanks and Tim Allen. Making it was enormous work. The crew grew to about 110 people, including 27 animators. Every character and set had to be built as a 3D model inside a computer, with controls for every eyebrow, finger and wobble.

Then each frame had to be rendered. Rendering means the computer calculates how light falls on every surface and what color each pixel should be. The finished film has 114,240 frames in 1,561 shots, and rendering them took about 800,000 machine hours on racks of Sun Microsystems computers running day and night. That works out to roughly seven hours of computer time per frame, on average. On a good day, the studio could finish less than 30 seconds of film.

Toy Story opened in the United States on 22 November 1995. It was the first feature-length film made entirely with computer animation, and it became the biggest box-office film of that year in the US. Lasseter received a Special Achievement Academy Award for leading the team. Within a decade, most big animated features were made with computers rather than hand-drawn cels, the method you read about in Part 15.

Look back at the half-century in this part. In 1950, a movie was light shining through a strip of film in a dark room, the same basic idea as in the 1890s. By 2000, people could record their own videos at home, sit in front of screens ten times bigger, and watch worlds that existed only as numbers in a computer. But one thing had not changed: most cameras, from family camcorders to IMAX rigs, still recorded the final picture on film or tape.

Yet the computer revolution was already reaching inside the camera itself. Back in 1975, in a laboratory at Kodak, the company that had put film into everyone's hands, a young engineer had quietly built a strange, toaster-sized camera that used no film at all.

deepDive: The widescreen wars of the 1950s left a lasting vocabulary: the aspect ratio, which is a picture's width divided by its height. Older films used the Academy ratio of about 1.37 to 1, close to the 4 to 3 shape of old TVs. Most American films then settled on 1.85 to 1, while anamorphic 'Scope' films use about 2.39 to 1. The math of anamorphic lenses is neat: a 2x squeeze lets a frame that is physically about 1.2 times as wide as tall carry an image about 2.4 times as wide as tall. The cost is that each horizontal detail is spread over half the film width, which is why early lenses needed careful design to avoid distortion like 'the mumps'. IMAX takes the opposite approach, adding area instead of squeezing: its 15-perforation 70mm frame, roughly 70 by 48 millimeters, has about ten times the area of a standard 35mm frame, which reduces visible grain when enlarged onto screens over 20 meters wide. Videotape required a different trick. The quantity that matters for recording is 'writing speed', the speed of the head relative to the tape. Quadruplex spun its heads so fast that the effective writing speed was around 1,500 inches per second, even though the tape itself crawled along at 15 inches per second. Home VCRs later used helical scanning, tilting the drum so each head wrote long diagonal stripes, which allowed smaller cassettes. Historians still debate why VHS beat Betamax. The usual explanations are longer recording time, lower prices and JVC's willingness to license VHS to many manufacturers, though some argue Sony's insistence on picture quality simply did not match what buyers wanted. For CGI, the debate is about credit and labels: Tron, Young Sherlock Holmes, The Abyss and Jurassic Park each claim a 'first' with a different definition, and Jurassic Park's success depended as much on animatronics as on computers, a balance many filmmakers still argue was the right one.
funFact: When stop-motion animator Phil Tippett saw ILM's computer dinosaurs for Jurassic Park, he joked 'I think I'm extinct', and Steven Spielberg liked the line so much he put it in the movie.
